entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
David of Kakheti, serving as Choreposcopus of the Eastern Georgian principality of Kakheti, governed from 976 until his death in 1010. His reign represents a critical period in the fragmented political landscape of medieval Georgia, where he staunchly resisted the centralizing ambitions of Bagrat III, the powerful Bagratid king who sought to unite all Georgian lands under a single crown. David's steadfast commitment to Kakhetian autonomy, despite facing a formidable opponent, ensured the principality's independence for several decades, thereby shaping the geopolitical contours of the Caucasus at the turn of the 11th century and delaying the complete unification of Georgia.

During his 34-year rule, David navigated a complex web of alliances and conflicts. Upon his accession, he inherited a principality that had historically maintained a precarious balance against larger powers. His most significant challenge was the burgeoning power of King Bagrat III, who, having united Kartli and Abkhazia, set his sights on Kakheti. David, demonstrating considerable diplomatic skill and military resolve, forged an alliance with Kvirike III of Tao-Klarjeti, another regional ruler wary of Bagrat's expansion. This strategic partnership allowed David to repel several attempts by Bagrat III to annex Kakheti, notably in the late 10th and early 11th centuries, ensuring the principality's distinct political identity persisted.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: David of Kakheti's 34-year reign significantly delayed the complete unification of Georgia under Bagrat III, thereby shaping the political landscape of the Caucasus for several decades. His successful resistance ensured the continuity of Kakhetian autonomy, influencing the timeline of Georgian state-building.
